title: SA/173/2013 of BILLOO Vs NAGAR PALIKA PARISHAD, MUSSOORIE, DISTRICT DEHRADUN THROUGH ITS EXECUTIVE OFFICER

paras.text:
HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
Second Appeal No. 173 of 2013
Billoo S/o Shri Lallu .....Appellant/Plaintiff
Versus
Nagar Palika Parishad and another ....Respondents
Present :
Mr. Inder Pal Kohli, Advocate for the plaintiff / appellant.
Mr. Bhuwan Bhatt, Advocate for the respondents.
 Dated: 10th September, 2020
JUDGEMENT
Hon'ble Sharad Kumar Sharma, J.
(Via Video Conferencing)
1. This is a plaintiff's Second Appeal, wherein, the plaintiff/
appellant, herein, has challenged the impugned judgements dated 6th
December, 2013, as rendered in Civil Appeal No. 49 of 2011, Billoo
Vs. Nagar Palika Parishad, Mussoorie and another, which stood
dismissed by the judgement of the learned District Judge, and as a
consequence thereto, it has resulted into an affirmation of the
judgement and decree dated 28th March, 2011, as rendered by the
Court of Civil Judge (Senior Division), Dehradun, in Original Suit
No. 519 of 2002, Billoo Vs. Nagar Palika Parishad and another, by
virtue of which, the Suit of the appellant for grant of decree of
permanent injunction, preferred by the plaintiff/ appellant was
dismissed. As a consequence thereto, in fact, the present Second
Appeal arises out of a concurrent judgement of the Court below.
2. The Second Appeal was admitted by the Coordinate
Bench of this Court by the order dated 27th December, 2013, and the
following substantial question of law was framed, which is quoted
hereunder :-
"Whether the respondent authorities are entitled to
evict the appellant/plaintiff without adopting due process of
law when admittedly the appellant/plaintiff was inducted in

2
the property in question by the respondent authorities
themselves"
3. While proceeding to hear the Counsel for the parties to
the present Second Appeal, and having given a thoughtful
consideration, this Court is of the view that it is a fit case, in which,
this Court, should exercise its power under Sub-section (4) of Section
100 of the CPC by formulating an additional substantial question of
law to the effect that "as to whether the judgement of the Appellate
Court suffered from the vices of non-compliance of the provisions
contained Order 41 Rule 31 of the CPC ?"
4. After having heard the learned counsel for the parties at
length, this Court is of the view that certain essential factual backdrop
of the case are required to be considered. The plaint case of the
plaintiff/appellant, herein, which was instituted by him before the
Court of Civil Judge (Senior Division) on 25th July, 2002, was to the
effect, that he had moved an application on 3rd January, 1995, for
allotment of a space wherefrom, he could operate his business after
establishment of a Khokha. It is an admitted case of the
plaintiff/appellant, herein, that his aforesaid application dated 3rd
January, 1995, was processed by the defendant/respondents and the
application thus preferred before plaintiff/appellant was accepted by
it, and subsequent thereto, an order was passed by the
defendant/respondent on 6th February, 1995, by virtue of which, a
small piece of land, having an area of 8 feet x 5 feet, situated near
Mosanic Lodge, which was situated near Roadways Bus Stop, was
licenced to be used by him, on the rent, which was payable @
Rs.2,000/- per annum. It is the case of the plaintiff/appellant, in the
Suit that under the aforesaid licence, which was initially granted for a
period of 11 months, he had constructed his Khokha and was
operating his business, by way of a Tea Stall called as 'Billoo Tea
Stall'.

3
5. Since the permission granted by the Nagar Palika; to the
appellant as a licensee, to use the particular land was for the
construction of Kohoka, the said decision was not welcomed by the
neighbourer Hotel Owner, named as Hari Raj Singh, the plaintiff's
case in the plaint is that Hari Raj Singh had forcefully demolished the
Kokha constructed on a land thus allotted to him on 6th September,
1999, as a consequence thereto, the petitioner contends that he has
approached the respondent, as well as the SDM for allotment of an
alternative land or place, from where he could run his shop.
6. The appellant's case is that yet again the respondent had
proceeded, to allot him an alternate vacant land measuring 25 feet x
10 feet near Mussoorie Bus Stand, where he had constructed the
Khokha and operated his business under the name and style of Billoo
Tea Stall and also got installed the water and electricity connection on
it. He further submitted that in pursuance to the terms and conditions
of the licence, he has remitted the rent for two years on 13th February,
1995, to the tune of Rs. 4,000/-.
7. The plaintiff/appellant in the Suit has come up with the
case; that thereafter the respondent for the reason best known to them
have neither extended the licence nor they have accepted the settled
annual rent, which was settled to be paid in terms of the licence made
in his favour by the respondents. He submits that the said conduct of
the respondents of not acceptance of the rent and having proceeded to
take an arbitrary act of forceful eviction of the appellant would be
contrary to law because admittedly the possession handed over of the
land to the appellant, where he has constructed his khokha cannot be
exclusively termed as to be as unauthorised occupant for the reason
being that his possession over the land where there existed khoka, was
as a consequence of the licence executed by the respondents in favour
of the plaintiff/appellant, and hence, he contends that when on 22nd
July, 2002, the respondents threatened to remove the Tea Stall by
force without resorting to due process of law, he filed a Suit on 25th

4
July, 2002, for the grant of decree of permanent injunction, which was
numbered as Suit No. 519 of 2002, Billoo Vs. Nagar Palika Parishad
and another.
8. In the said Suit, in the description of the property, it had
specifically defined the chauhadi of the same, at the foot of the plaint
describing the details of the property, which was licensed to the
plaintiff/appellant by the defendant/respondents. In response to the
pleadings raised in the written statement, the defendant/respondents,
herein, had filed their written statement on 23rd September, 2002,
denying the plaint averments and further submitting that the
proceeding to the Suit itself was not maintainable on account of the
fact that there was non compliance of the provisions contained under
Section 326 of the U.P. Municipalities Act, and furthermore that the
Suit suffered from the vices of mis-joinder of the parties, as there
was no cause of action or relief sought as against the defendant No. 2,
who was impleaded as party to the proceedings, without there being
any cause against him.
9. In response to the written statement, the plaintiff/
appellant had filed his replication and, as a consequence thereto, the
Court of Civil Judge (Senior Division), after the exchange of the
pleadings had formulated the following issues under Order 14 of Code
of Civil Procedure :-

10. In support of his contention, the plaintiff had placed on
record the list of documents by way of paper No. 8 Ga, which
included the rent receipts, the application made by the
plaintiff/appellant for the permission to use the land i.e. paper 11A/1,
the correspondence by virtue of the registered letter, the water tax bill,
the electricity bill, as paper Nos. 12A and 13Ka respectively, the
notice, photographs, etc., in order to substantiate his case in Suit,
against the act of forceful eviction of the plaintiff/appellant.
11. The learned Trial Court, after considering the aforesaid
argument and the evidence adduced by the parties, had decided the
Suit and had dismissed the same by the judgement dated 28th March,
2011. What would be relevant to point out at this juncture is that on
scrutiny of the judgement as had been rendered and placed under
challenge, the issue pertaining to non compliance of Section 326 of
the Municipalities Act, was answered in favour of the
plaintiff/appellant by the learned Trial Court while deciding issue No.
5, holding thereof that the plaintiff/appellant did issue a notice, i.e.
paper 20 Ga, about two months prior to the institution of the Suit,
hence there was an apparent compliance of the provisions contained
under Section 326 of the Municipalities Act. It further observed that
since the plaintiff/appellant has failed to establish that he was the
principal allottee of the land in dispute, which was described at the

6
foot of the plaint, the issue Nos. 1 and 2; was decided against him, as
having failed to establish that the specified piece of land described at
the foot of the plaint was allotted by the Nagar Palika, in favour of the
plaintiff/appellant in the year 1995.
12. Be that as it may. On scrutiny of the impugned
judgements, one aspect which is quite apparent, is that there is nothing
on record by way of evidence brought by the defendant/respondents,
to show that prior to thereof taking of an action, of making an effort
for removal of the possession of the plaintiff/appellant on 22nd July,
2002, they had ever issued any notices to the plaintiff. Admittedly,
the issue No. 3, which was decided by the Trial Court, it was held that
the licence was executed in favour of the plaintiff in the year 1995
though initially for 11 months, meaning thereby, as per opinion of this
Court, the plaintiff/appellant was in a permissive possession of the
disputed property under the strength of the licence, which was granted
in his favour on 10th February, 1995. Hence, in the absence of there
being any prior notice issued by the respondents, directing the
plaintiff/appellant to vacate the premises, nor there was any prior
notice of terminating the licence granted to him on 10.02.1995, by the
respondents, hence, under the basic norms of law, the forceful
eviction runs contrary to the basic ethics and norms of law, because
even otherwise it is settled that even an unauthorised occupant cannot
be evicted from the land without a resort to due process of law. This is
one of the substantial questions, which was formulated by the learned
Co-ordinate Bench of this Court when the Appeal was admitted.
Hence, it is answered in favour of the plaintiff/appellant.
13. On the dismissal of the Suit, the matter travelled to a
Civil Appeal under Section 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure, being
Civil Appeal No. 49 of 2011, which too, as per the opinion of this
Court, was cryptically dismissed, without considering all the
prospective and the rival contentions raised by the parties while
deciding the appeal. Even apparently, if the Appellate Court's

7
judgement is scrutinized, in fact, it reflects that there was an apparent
non compliance of the provisions contained under Order 41 Rule 31
of the CPC, which is quite apparent from the finding itself which has
been recorded because there was no point of determination, which is
reflected to have been formulated, nor the same has been answered by
the Appellate Court at all, rather the only contribution made by the
Appellate Court, while deciding the Regular Appeal, which is the last
Court of fact and evidence, it ought to have considered the rival
contentions, formulated the point of determination, answered the same
on appreciation of evidence and then only it could have decided the
appeal rather than cursorily contributing a finding only in the last
paragraph of the judgment for the purposes to sustain his judgement
of dismissal of the Civil Appeal.
14. This Court of the view that as far as the manner, in which
the judgement has been rendered by the Appellate Court, it apparently
runs absolutely contrary to the provisions contained under Order 41
Rule 31 of the CPC. In that view of the matter, the aforesaid question
which has been formulated by this Court today, while exercising my
power under Sub-section (4) of Section 100 of the CPC, is answered
in favour of the plaintiff /appellant, to the effect that the judgment of
first Appellate Court suffers from legal lacuna of non compliance of
Order 41 Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
15. As far as the question, on which, the Appeal was
admitted, about the prior issuance of the notice by the Nagar Palika
before making any effort for forcefully evicting the plaintiff/appellant
from the place, which was admittedly licenced to him, there is no
evidence of any nature whatsoever on record to establish that any
prior notice was given to the plaintiff/appellant before resorting to
any step, being taken by the Nagar Palika for getting him evicted from
the land, which was allotted to him for running his shop (Tea Stall),
where he has constructed his Khokha.

8
16. Accordingly, in the absence of their being any evidence
on record to the contrary, the question formulated on 27th December,
2013, that the respondents have proceeded to make an effort to evict
the appellant without adopting the due process of law is also answered
in favour of the plaintiff. Holding thereof that Suit ought to have
decreed by injuncting the defendant/respondent from resorting to any
act of forceful eviction of the plaintiff/appellant.
17. In view of the aforesaid reasonings, since the
judgements, under challenge, apparently suffers from vices of non
adherence of the procedure permissible under law for evicting the
appellant, who was admittedly a licensee in pursuance to the licence
executed in his favour on 10th February, 1995, it is the place where his
Khokha exists, from where he is running his business in the name and
style of Billoo Tea Stall, the normal norms of law contemplated and it
was expected that the Nagar Palika, which is a statutory body created
under an Act, if at all, wants to get the accommodation vacated, it
ought to have issued the prior notice to the plaintiff/appellant before
making any effort for getting him evicted from the property in dispute.
Having not done so, the action of the Nagar Palika would be arbitrary
and illegal in the eyes of law.
18. For the aforesaid reasons, the Second Appeal is allowed,
the Suit preferred by the plaintiff/appellant would stand decreed to the
following effect:
"If the defendant/respondents at all contemplate to take any
action of evicting the plaintiff/appellant from the land, which
was licensed to him and from where he is running his business,
they could only do so after resorting to the process
contemplated under law and in particular the provisions
contained under U.P. Municipalities Act."

9
19. Subject to the aforesaid observation, the Suit stands
decreed. It will be open for the defendant/respondents to proceed to
evict, if at all required and permissible under law, only after resorting
to the due process of law. For the aforesaid reasons, the Second
Appeal stands allowed the impugned judgements and decree passed
by both the Courts below are hereby quashed.
20. However, there would be no order as to costs.
(Sharad Kumar Sharma, J.)
